warmup.q: An Iceberg table holds 300,000 payments in 3 Parquet files of about 1 MB, one per day. A MERGE INTO refunds 30 payments, 10 in each file. The table has default settings. Roughly how much data does the commit write?
options: A few KB: only the 30 changed rows
About 3 MB: all three files, rewritten with the changes
Nothing new: Iceberg edits the 30 rows inside the files
About 1 MB: the one file it rewrites first
warmup.why: Parquet files can't be edited in place, and Iceberg's default for MERGE, UPDATE and DELETE is copy-on-write: every file that holds a changed row is rewritten whole. Here that's all three files, about 3 MB, to change 30 rows. "A few KB" is what merge-on-read writes instead, and this lesson shows the price readers pay for it.

sections.h: Files never change, so a correction rewrites a file or writes a delete
sections.html:
Lesson 11 (Lakehouse tables with Apache Iceberg) built a table out of files that are written once and never changed, plus metadata that lists them. Appends fit that model perfectly. Corrections don't, and a warehouse takes them for granted: lesson 10's type 2 dimension closes a version with an UPDATE. This lesson builds the three things a table of immutable files needs to behave like a warehouse table over time: row-level changes, maintenance that keeps files few and large, and a catalog that holds the pointer. Every evening the card network sends your payments company a chargeback file: 30 captured payments that are now refunded. In Oracle you would run UPDATE payments SET status = 'REFUNDED' WHERE payment_id IN (...) and the database would change 30 rows in place. In a lakehouse those 30 rows sit inside Parquet files, and a Parquet file can't be edited. Its column chunks are compressed, and its footer records their sizes, offsets and min/max values (lesson 5, Columnar files: Parquet internals and pushdown). Change one value and all of that is wrong.

So any change has to be written as new files. The SQL for it is MERGE INTO, which joins a batch of changes to the table on a key and says what to do with matches and non-matches (the worked example below builds one). Under the SQL, there are two ways to write the files, and the stepper shows both.

Version 1 is copy-on-write. Find every data file that holds a row to change, read it whole, and write a new copy with the change applied. The commit swaps the old files for the new ones. In the Try it, 30 refunds spread over three daily files of 100,000 rows rewrote all three: 3.1 MB written and 299,970 unchanged rows copied to change 30. Readers don't notice anything: the table is still plain data files. That's Iceberg's default, and it's right for a table that is read far more often than it changes. It breaks when changes are small and frequent. A correction feed that runs every 5 minutes against 512 MB files (Iceberg's default target size) rewrites gigabytes an hour to change a few hundred rows.

Version 2 is merge-on-read. Leave the data files alone. Write the new versions of the 30 rows into a small new data file, and write a delete file that says which old rows no longer count. Spark writes position deletes: pairs of (data file path, row position), such as "row 1,000 of the day 1 file". The same 30 refunds wrote 6.4 KB of new rows and 7.4 KB of delete files. The cost moves to the reader. Every scan of a data file must now also read the delete files that apply to it and skip the listed rows. Iceberg also defines equality deletes, which name a value instead of a position ("payment 1042 is gone"). A streaming writer such as Flink in upsert mode writes them because it doesn't have to find the row first; readers then compare every row against them, which is slower still.

The newest format version tightens the reader's side. Over many batches, one data file can collect many position delete files. Iceberg format v3 replaces them with deletion vectors: one compact bitmap of deleted positions per data file, stored in a Puffin file (Iceberg's container format for blobs like this). A later delete in the same file merges into the existing vector, so a reader loads at most one small bitmap per data file. In the Try it, the v3 table stored 3 vectors in one 1.7 KB Puffin file.

You pick per table, and per operation, with three properties: write.merge.mode, write.update.mode and write.delete.mode, each copy-on-write or merge-on-read. Use copy-on-write for tables that change in rare, large batches. Use merge-on-read, on format v3 where your engines support it, for frequent small corrections, and pay the reader's bill with compaction (next section).

refs.title: Iceberg spec: row-level deletes and deletion vectors

sections.h: Small files and delete files pile up until you compact
sections.html:
Merge-on-read and streaming have the same side effect: many small files. Lesson 4 (Hive: SQL on files, partitions and the metastore) measured it on a plain folder: the same rows as 350 small files took about ten times longer to query than as 7 files, because every file costs an open, a footer read and, on S3, a request with its own latency. A table format removes the folder listing, but not the per-file cost. Each data file still has to be opened, and each delete file has to be read and applied.

Watch it build up in the Try it. A stream commits every few minutes, so twelve commits leave twelve small files for one day. Three correction batches add three more small data files and twelve delete files. The day's 60,000 rows now live in 15 data files of about 44 KB each, and a full scan plans 15 file tasks that must apply 12 delete files. The table also has 15 snapshots, and each one is a little more metadata to plan through.

The fix is compaction: rewrite many small files into a few large ones, applying the deletes on the way. In Iceberg it's a procedure you call from Spark:

CALL lake.system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'pay.stream',
  options => map('min-input-files', '2', 'delete-file-threshold', '1'))

The default strategy, bin-pack, groups files by partition and packs them into files near the target size (512 MB by default). min-input-files sets how many small files make a group worth rewriting (5 by default), and delete-file-threshold makes any data file with at least that many deletes attached a candidate. A sort strategy also re-sorts rows on the way, which makes the min/max statistics from lesson 5 sharper. In the Try it, compaction turned 15 data files and 12 delete files into 1 file of about 630 KB. The rows didn't change, and the new snapshot says so: its operation is replace, which tells readers the data is the same and only the layout moved.

Compaction is an ordinary commit, so it can race with writers (lesson 11). If a correction lands on a file while compaction is rewriting it, one of the two commits fails its check and has to run again. Run compaction as a scheduled job, partition by partition, skip the partitions a stream is still writing, and set the option partial-progress.enabled on big tables so a failure doesn't throw away hours of work. Two smaller procedures complete the set: rewrite_position_delete_files compacts delete files, and rewrite_manifests repacks the manifests after many small commits.

refs.title: Iceberg maintenance: compaction, expiring snapshots, orphan files

sections.h: Old snapshots and orphan files hold disk until you clean up
sections.html:
Compaction makes the table fast, but it doesn't make it smaller. After the compaction in the Try it, the current snapshot lists 3 data files and the data/ folder holds 18. The other 15 are still listed by older snapshots, and lesson 11 promised that every snapshot can be read with VERSION AS OF. Iceberg can't delete a file while any snapshot still lists it. Every append, every correction and every compaction leaves the previous files behind.

The cleanup is expiring snapshots. expire_snapshots removes old snapshots from the table's metadata, then deletes every file that only those snapshots used: data files, delete files, manifests and manifest lists. By default it expires snapshots older than 5 days and always keeps the newest one. In the Try it, expiring everything but the newest snapshot deleted 15 data files, 5 manifests and 5 manifest lists, and data/ went from 18 files to 3. The price is history: time travel to an expired snapshot now fails with Cannot find snapshot with ID .... So the retention you choose is a business decision. If auditors may ask what a settlement report read last month, keep at least a month of snapshots, or tag that snapshot so expiry skips it.

One more kind of garbage has no snapshot at all. A job that crashes after writing data files but before its commit leaves orphan files: files in the table's folder that no snapshot ever listed (lesson 11's stepper showed how they arise). Expiry can't find them, because it only deletes files that snapshots name. remove_orphan_files works the other way: it lists the folder and deletes every file that no snapshot references. That is dangerous in one specific case. A job that is writing right now has files on disk that aren't committed yet, and they look exactly like orphans. So the procedure only deletes files older than a cut-off, 3 days by default, and refuses anything under 24 hours. In the Try it, a file from a job that crashed three days ago was removed, and a file being written right now was kept.

Run both on a schedule, after compaction: compact, then expire, then remove orphans once in a while. On object storage, deletes also cost requests, and the bucket bill only drops after expiry runs.

sections.h: The catalog holds the pointer that makes a commit atomic
sections.html:
Lesson 11's commit was a compare-and-swap of one pointer: "the table is now v4.metadata.json, if it is still v3". The thing that stores that pointer, and makes the swap atomic, is the catalog. It also answers the question every engine asks first: what tables exist, and where is each one's current metadata?

Version 1 is the Hadoop catalog lesson 11 used. The pointer is the newest metadata file in a folder, and the swap is a rename that fails if the target exists. That needs a file system with an atomic rename. Your laptop and HDFS have one. S3 doesn't, so this catalog is for learning.

Version 2 puts the pointer in a database. The Hive Metastore (lesson 4's catalog, a service in front of a relational database) can hold it as a property of the Hive table. Iceberg's JDBC catalog is the simplest to read: one row per table in a table called iceberg_tables, and a commit is a single SQL statement.

UPDATE iceberg_tables
SET metadata_location = ?, previous_metadata_location = ?
WHERE catalog_name = ? AND table_namespace = ? AND table_name = ?
  AND metadata_location = ?        -- the version this writer started from

That is the same optimistic lock you'd write on an Oracle ledger: if another writer moved the pointer first, the WHERE matches no row, zero rows change, and Iceberg throws CommitFailedException. The Try it runs this catalog on a SQLite file and shows the row after each commit.

Version 2 has a cost: every engine needs the database driver, its credentials, and the right Iceberg library version. Version 3 puts the catalog behind an HTTP API, the Iceberg REST catalog protocol. The client asks GET /v1/namespaces/pay/tables/payments and gets back the table's metadata, including the pointer. To commit, it sends POST to the same path with a list of requirements, such as "the current snapshot is still 5087...", and a list of updates. The server checks the requirements and applies the updates atomically, or answers 409 Conflict. Because the server stands between the engines and storage, it can also hand each client short-lived storage credentials for just that table, and apply access rules in one place. Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB and most other engines speak this protocol.

You don't write a REST catalog yourself. Apache Polaris, an Apache top-level project since 2026, implements it. Unity Catalog OSS serves it too, since release 0.7, next to its Delta Lake API. Cloud providers run their own. Pick the one your platform team already operates, and check that every engine you use can reach it.

Prints the catalog's row for the * table after each commit, then shows a commit from a stale version being refused. */ fun main() { val db = File("build/l10/catalog.db").apply { delete() } val spark = demoSpark( "spark.sql.catalog.shop" to "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog", "spark.sql.catalog.shop.type" to "jdbc", "spark.sql.catalog.shop.uri" to "jdbc:sqlite:${db.absolutePath}", "spark.sql.catalog.shop.warehouse" to File(WAREHOUSE, "shop").absolutePath, ) fun catalogRow(label: String) = DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:sqlite:${db.absolutePath}").use { c -> c.createStatement().executeQuery( "SELECT table_namespace, table_name, metadata_location, previous_metadata_location FROM iceberg_tables" ).use { rs -> while (rs.next()) { fun name(i: Int) = rs.getString(i)?.substringAfterLast('/')?.replace(Regex("^(\\d+)-[0-9a-f-]{36}"), "$1-<uuid>") ?: "null" println("$label: ${rs.getString(1)}.${rs.getString(2)} -> ${name(3)} (previous: ${name(4)})") } } } spark.sql("CREATE TABLE shop.pay.payments ($PAYMENT_COLUMNS) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))") catalogRow("after CREATE TABLE") payments(spark, 0, 1_000).writeTo("shop.pay.payments").append() catalogRow("after the 1st append") payments(spark, 1_000, 1_000).writeTo("shop.pay.payments").append() catalogRow("after the 2nd append") // two writers load the same version; A commits first, then B tries from its stale base val catalog = Spark3Util.loadIcebergCatalog(spark, "shop") val id = TableIdentifier.of("pay", "payments") val a = (catalog.loadTable(id) as HasTableOperations).operations() val b = (catalog.loadTable(id) as HasTableOperations).operations() val baseA = a.current() val baseB = b.current() a.commit(baseA, TableMetadata.buildFrom(baseA).setProperties(mapOf("owner" to "settlement")).build()) catalogRow("after writer A's commit") try { b.commit(baseB, TableMetadata.buildFrom(baseB).setProperties(mapOf("owner" to "fraud")).build()) } catch (e: CommitFailedException) { println("writer B, from the old version: CommitFailedException: ${e.message!!.replace(Regex("/\\S+/"), "")}") } catalogRow("after writer B's attempt") println("rows: %,d".format(spark.table("shop.pay.payments").count())) spark.stop() }

try.expect:
after CREATE TABLE: pay.payments -> 00000-<uuid>.metadata.json (previous: null)
after the 1st append: pay.payments -> 00001-<uuid>.metadata.json (previous: 00000-<uuid>.metadata.json)
after the 2nd append: pay.payments -> 00002-<uuid>.metadata.json (previous: 00001-<uuid>.metadata.json)
after writer A's commit: pay.payments -> 00003-<uuid>.metadata.json (previous: 00002-<uuid>.metadata.json)
writer B, from the old version: CommitFailedException: Cannot commit: stale table metadata
after writer B's attempt: pay.payments -> 00003-<uuid>.metadata.json (previous: 00002-<uuid>.metadata.json)
rows: 2,000

Each commit wrote a new metadata file and moved the row's metadata_location to it, keeping the old one in previous_metadata_location. Writer A's commit moved the pointer from 00002 to 00003. Writer B started from 00002 too; its UPDATE ... WHERE metadata_location = <00002> matched no row, so Iceberg threw CommitFailedException and the row didn't move. The table is still 2,000 rows. Your sqlite3 output shows the same row with full paths, something like this (paths shortened):

              catalog_name: shop
           table_namespace: pay
                table_name: payments
         metadata_location: .../warehouse/shop/pay/payments/metadata/00003-8190629d-....metadata.json
previous_metadata_location: .../warehouse/shop/pay/payments/metadata/00002-3bfa617f-....metadata.json

That row is the whole catalog for this table. Delete it and every engine loses the table, though every file is still on disk.

sections.h: Delta Lake, Hudi and DuckLake make the same trade differently
sections.html:
Iceberg isn't the only table format. Delta Lake and Apache Hudi make the same trade with different files, and DuckLake moves the metadata into a database. All of them keep immutable Parquet data files, list them in metadata, and commit by one atomic step that either happens or doesn't.

Delta Lake keeps a log instead of a tree. Every commit is a numbered JSON file in _delta_log/: 00000000000000000007.json lists the files the commit added and removed. A reader replays the log from the last checkpoint, a Parquet summary that Delta writes every few commits. A commit is "create file number 8 if it doesn't exist yet": two writers can't both create it, so one wins. On S3 that is exactly what If-None-Match has offered since 2024 (lesson 11); Delta's S3 documentation still asks for a single writing driver per table, or a DynamoDB table for mutual exclusion. Delta has copy-on-write, merge-on-read through deletion vectors, MERGE INTO and compaction (OPTIMIZE), with different names for the same ideas. It's the default format on Databricks. Delta 4.4 (4.4.1 is current, from October 2026) supports Spark 4.0.1, 4.1 and 4.2. Its UniForm feature writes Iceberg metadata next to Delta's, so Iceberg readers can read a Delta table, though UniForm's Iceberg module doesn't support Spark 4.2 yet. Delta 4.3 added Unity Catalog's Delta REST API, part of a move to catalog-managed tables, where the catalog rather than the log in storage coordinates commits.

Apache Hudi grew out of upsert-heavy ingestion: change data capture from databases into the lake. It names the two write strategies as table types, COPY_ON_WRITE and MERGE_ON_READ, and keeps an index from record key to file, so an upsert finds its row without scanning. Hudi 1.2 (1.2.1 is current) added VECTOR, VARIANT and BLOB types and support for the Lance file format, and ships bundles for Spark 3.3 to 4.1. Choose it when your workload is mostly keyed upserts from a CDC stream and your team already knows it.

DuckLake, from the DuckDB project (1.0 in April 2026; 1.1 ships with DuckDB 2.0), asks a sharper question. If a catalog is a database anyway, why keep the rest of the metadata in files? DuckLake stores snapshots, schemas, file lists and statistics as rows in a SQL database (PostgreSQL, SQLite or DuckDB), and data in Parquet. A commit is one database transaction, so a small change writes a few rows instead of a manifest, a manifest list and a metadata file, and multi-table commits come for free. The trade is that every reader needs that database, its commit rate is bounded by the database's (PostgreSQL manages thousands of transactions a second), and far fewer engines read DuckLake than read Iceberg.

For a payments company starting today, Iceberg with a REST catalog is the safe default: the most engines read and write it, and lesson 15 relies on it. Pick Delta if you run on Databricks, and keep DuckLake in mind for a small team that lives in DuckDB.

analogy: Think of a ledger kept in pen in bound notebooks. You never erase a line. To correct a payment you have two choices. You can copy the whole page out again with the fix in it and tear out the old page: that's copy-on-write, and the notebook stays clean to read. Or you can leave the page alone and add a slip at the back that says "line 12 on page 40 is void, see the new line on page 97": that's merge-on-read, quick to write, and every reader now has to check the slips. A deletion vector is one slip per page instead of a pile. Compaction is the night clerk who copies messy pages out clean, and expiring snapshots is shredding the old pages once nobody may ask for them. The catalog is the index card at the front that says which notebook is current. The analogy breaks at concurrency: two clerks can't write in one notebook at once, but two Iceberg writers can work at the same time and only find out at the commit, when the catalog's compare-and-swap lets one of them through.
world: Your payments ledger in Oracle takes corrections all day: refunds, chargebacks, voids, late captures. When the analytics copy of that ledger moves to Iceberg, those corrections arrive as a Kafka topic or a CDC stream, and each micro-batch becomes a MERGE INTO. Make that table merge-on-read on format v3, and schedule a Temporal workflow (or the Airflow job your data team runs) that compacts yesterday's partitions at night, then expires snapshots older than your audit window. The JDBC catalog's commit is the same optimistic lock you already write in your services, UPDATE ... WHERE version = :v, and a failed commit is the same signal: someone else changed it first, reload and retry. When finance asks which data a settlement report read, the answer is a snapshot id, and expiry decides how long that answer stays checkable.
mistake: The common mistake is turning on merge-on-read, or pointing a stream at a table, and never scheduling the maintenance. Nothing fails. Writes are fast, every query still returns the right rows, and the table gets slower each day as delete files and small files pile up, while the bucket grows because no snapshot is ever expired. Teams notice months later, when a daily report that took two minutes takes forty and the table holds two million files. People skip it because Iceberg feels like a database, and a database cleans up after itself; Iceberg is a format plus libraries, and nothing runs unless you run it. The fix is three scheduled jobs from the day the table is created: compact recent partitions (rewrite_data_files, with delete-file-threshold for merge-on-read tables), expire snapshots past your retention, and remove orphan files weekly with the default 3-day cut-off. Watch the table's health with the data_files and delete_files metadata tables, the way the lab does.

compare.title: One append in Iceberg and in Delta Lake (schematic, names shortened)

a.label: Apache Iceberg
a.title: a tree of metadata files, plus a catalog

  data/created_at_day=2026-11-03/
    00000-....parquet             new data file
  metadata/
    3f2c...-m0.avro               new manifest: the new file, with stats

    v8.metadata.json              new table metadata: snapshot 5087... is current

commit: the catalog swaps its pointer v7 -> v8,
        only if it still says v7

b.label: Delta Lake
b.title: a numbered log of JSON commits
b.html:
payments/
  dt=2026-11-03/
    part-00000-....parquet        new data file
  _delta_log/
    00000000000000000006.json     earlier commits
    00000000000000000007.json     new: {"add": {"path": "dt=.../part-....parquet", ...}}
                                       {"commitInfo": {"operation": "WRITE", ...}}
    000...010.checkpoint.parquet  every few commits: the whole state, for fast replay

commit: create 00000000000000000007.json,
        only if no one created it first

compare.note: Both formats write the data file first, where no reader can see it, and both commit with one step that fails if someone else got there first. Iceberg's step is a swap in a catalog, and a reader starts from the catalog's pointer and walks down a tree. Delta's step is creating the next numbered file, and a reader lists _delta_log/, loads the newest checkpoint and replays the JSON files after it. Iceberg's manifests can be shared between snapshots and pruned by partition ranges before they're opened; Delta's log is simpler to read by hand. Delta 4.x can also let a catalog coordinate commits, and its UniForm feature writes Iceberg metadata beside the log.

worked.title: Apply the nightly chargeback file with one MERGE

steps.say: Stage the corrections as a view, one row per payment. The card network can send the same payment twice in one file (a chargeback, then its reversal). MERGE allows at most one source row per target row, so keep only the newest per payment_id.
steps.code: CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW corrections AS SELECT payment_id, status, amount_cents, created_at, merchant_id, card_country, currency FROM ( SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY payment_id ORDER BY received_at DESC) AS rn FROM chargeback_file ) WHERE rn = 1;

steps.say: Write the MERGE. Match on the key, delete voids, update everything else that matched, and insert payments the table has never seen (late captures). Spark plans this as a join of the small view against the table, so a broadcast of the corrections and partition pruning on created_at keep it cheap.
steps.code: MERGE INTO lake.pay.payments t USING corrections c ON t.payment_id = c.payment_id WHEN MATCHED AND c.status = 'VOID' THEN DELETE WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.status = c.status, t.amount_cents = c.amount_cents WHEN NOT MATCHED AND c.status <> 'VOID' THEN INSERT *;

steps.say: If you skipped the first step and a payment appears twice, Spark stops before writing anything, with MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION: one target row matched several source rows, and it won't guess which wins. Nothing is committed, so you can fix the view and rerun.
steps.code:
-- [MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION] The ON search condition of the MERGE statement
-- matched a single row from the target table with multiple rows of the source table.

steps.say: Check what the commit did. The snapshot summary records it: for a merge-on-read table, delete files added and rows inserted; for copy-on-write, files removed and rows copied.
steps.code: SELECT summary['spark.merge-into.num-target-rows-updated'] AS updated, summary['spark.merge-into.num-target-rows-deleted'] AS voided, summary['spark.merge-into.num-target-rows-inserted'] AS inserted, summary['added-delete-files'] AS delete_files FROM lake.pay.payments.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at DESC LIMIT 1;

steps.say: Leave the table healthy for tomorrow: the maintenance job compacts the partitions the merge touched, then expires snapshots past the retention window.
steps.code: CALL lake.system.rewrite_data_files( table => 'pay.payments', where => 'created_at >= "2026-11-01"', options => map('delete-file-threshold', '1')); CALL lake.system.expire_snapshots(table => 'pay.payments', older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-10-08 00:00:00');

lab.title: Correct payments, then compact and clean up
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail on TODOs. Each test class makes a Hadoop catalog called l12 in a JUnit temp folder, and the tests read the snapshot summaries, the data_files and delete_files metadata tables, and the files on disk.
Write PaymentCorrections.create: the payments table with days(created_at) partitioning and four table properties, the format version and the three write.*.mode properties.

Write applyCorrections: register the corrections as a temp view, run one MERGE INTO with the three clauses its KDoc lists, and return the newest snapshot's summary. The tests check that copy-on-write removed 3 data files and copied 2,997 rows, that merge-on-read on v2 wrote 3 position delete files and touched no data file, and that v3 wrote 3 deletion vectors in one Puffin file.

Write TableMaintenance.health from the metadata tables, then compact and expireSnapshots with the procedures. The test table has 12 small data files and 3 delete files; after compact it must have one file per day and no delete files, with the same rows.
The expiry test counts Parquet files on disk before and after, and checks that time travel to the first snapshot fails once it's expired.
hints: spark.sql("SELECT summary FROM $name.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at DESC LIMIT 1").first().getJavaMap<String, String>(0).toMap().

The catalog is name.substringBefore('.') and the procedure's table is name.substringAfter('.'): CALL l12.system.rewrite_data_files(table => 'ops.t', options => map('min-input-files', '2', 'delete-file-threshold', '1', 'remove-dangling-deletes', 'true')). Read the result with first().getAs<Int>("rewritten_data_files_count").

expire_snapshots takes older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-11-07 10:15:00.000' (in the session time zone, spark.sql.session.timeZone) and retain_last => 1; its result has deleted_data_files_count as a Long.

drill.title: Corrections and maintenance from memory
drill.prompt: From memory, write: the table properties that make an Iceberg table use merge-on-read for MERGE, UPDATE and DELETE on format v3; a MERGE INTO that applies refunds from a view refunds(payment_id, amount_cents); and the three maintenance calls, in the order you'd schedule them. Then say which of the three can make time travel fail.

answer.html: ALTER TABLE lake.pay.payments SET TBLPROPERTIES ( 'format-version' = '3', 'write.merge.mode' = 'merge-on-read', 'write.update.mode' = 'merge-on-read', 'write.delete.mode' = 'merge-on-read'); MERGE INTO lake.pay.payments t USING refunds r ON t.payment_id = r.payment_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.status = 'REFUNDED', t.amount_cents = r.amount_cents; -- 1. compact: fewer, bigger files, deletes applied (a 'replace' snapshot) CALL lake.system.rewrite_data_files(table => 'pay.payments', options => map('delete-file-threshold', '1')); -- 2. expire: drop old snapshots and the files only they used (ends time travel to them) CALL lake.system.expire_snapshots(table => 'pay.payments', older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-10-08 00:00:00'); -- 3. orphans: files no snapshot ever listed, older than the cut-off (3 days by default) CALL lake.system.remove_orphan_files(table => 'pay.payments'); -- only expire_snapshots ends time travel: compaction keeps the old snapshots, -- and orphan files were never in any snapshot

recap: Data files never change, so a row-level change writes new files. Copy-on-write rewrites every file that holds a changed row: slow writes, simple reads. It's Iceberg's default.
Merge-on-read writes the new rows plus delete files: position deletes (file, row) in format v2, one deletion vector per data file in v3. Writes are cheap and readers merge until compaction.
MERGE INTO joins a batch of changes to the table on a key and commits once. Each target row may match at most one source row.

rewrite_data_files compacts small files and applies deletes in a replace snapshot. expire_snapshots deletes files only old snapshots used, and ends time travel to them. remove_orphan_files deletes uncommitted leftovers older than a safe cut-off.

The catalog holds each table's pointer and does the compare-and-swap: a rename (Hadoop), a conditional UPDATE (JDBC), or an HTTP commit with requirements (the REST protocol, served by Polaris, Unity Catalog and cloud catalogs).
Delta Lake commits numbered JSON log files, Hudi targets keyed upserts, and DuckLake keeps all metadata in a SQL database. Iceberg with a REST catalog is the safe default.

explain.prompt: Explain to a colleague why your merge-on-read payments table needs three scheduled jobs, by following one batch of 30 refunds from the MERGE to the day its old files disappear.
explain.answer: The MERGE can't edit Parquet files, so on a merge-on-read table it writes the refunded versions of the 30 rows into a small new data file and a delete file per touched data file that says which old rows no longer count (on format v3, one deletion vector per data file). The commit is cheap, but every reader of those days now opens the data files, the new small files and the delete files, and merges them. After a day of batches that's dozens of extra files per partition. The first job, compaction (rewrite_data_files), reads each partition's files with their deletes and writes a few clean, large files in a replace snapshot, so reads are fast again. But nothing has been deleted: the snapshots from before compaction still list the old files, which is what makes time travel work. The second job, expire_snapshots, removes snapshots older than our retention and deletes every file only they used; from then on, time travel to those snapshots fails, so the retention must cover what auditors may ask about. The third job, remove_orphan_files, catches files that no snapshot ever listed, like the output of a MERGE that crashed before its commit. It only touches files older than a cut-off, 3 days by default, because files of a job that is still running look exactly like orphans.

deeper.html:
Equality deletes trade write cost for read cost even harder than position deletes. A writer that only knows a key, such as a Flink job applying upserts from a CDC stream, can write "delete every row where payment_id = 1042" without finding the row first. Every reader of every older data file in that partition must then check its rows against those values. Iceberg applies equality deletes only to data files with a lower sequence number (written earlier). Compact tables that receive them often.

Isolation for row-level changes is stricter than for appends. Lesson 11's appends could always re-apply after losing a race. A MERGE read some files and decided what to change from them, so if another commit changed those same files first, simply re-applying could lose an update. Iceberg's write.merge.isolation-level (and the update and delete variants) defaults to serializable: before committing, the writer checks whether any conflicting files were added or deleted since it started, and fails if so. snapshot isolation checks less and allows more concurrency.

The REST protocol keeps growing. Besides loading and committing tables, servers can plan scans on the server side (Iceberg 1.11), and Iceberg 1.12 added idempotency keys, so a client whose commit request timed out can retry without committing twice. Some servers also federate other catalogs, and Hive's documentation describes a REST catalog served by the Hive Metastore itself, so an existing metastore can speak the new protocol.

DuckLake has a small-change trick of its own, data inlining: inserts below a row limit are stored as rows in the catalog database instead of as tiny Parquet files, and a flush writes them to Parquet later. That attacks the small-files problem at the source.
